theme: LLM agent simulation, survey response fidelity, distributional validation, calibration and extrapolation
selection_note: Seven sources were selected: three core full-text reads (Argyle, Bisbee, Park) and four targeted reads on economic-agent calibration, experimental replication, probability sampling, and uncertainty calibration. Pages and author or institutional sources were opened. Shell PDF retrieval was blocked by sandbox DNS; no local PDF or SHA-256 is claimed. The parent task will centralize retrieval and hashing.

sources.title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
evidence_locations: arXiv PDF pp. 4–15; especially algorithmic fidelity and silicon sampling
findings: The paper defines algorithmic fidelity as reproducing target group response distributions and relations, and demonstrates that suitable conditioning can produce different political and public-opinion response patterns.

The authors explicitly distinguish population-level sample simulation from faithfully simulating a particular individual; conditioning on persona attributes does not guarantee individual coherence or fidelity in a new domain.
limitations: The empirical setting is U.S. political attitudes and public opinion, not household inflation expectations or SCE Q8/Q9.
The work does not establish that demographic labels alone recover economically meaningful heterogeneity or within-person probability densities.
sources.project_use: Use algorithmic fidelity as a validation target: compare weighted response distributions and cross-question relationships, not only the national mean or persona plausibility. Treat the paper as a design precedent, not evidence that the current demographic-only SCE agents are faithful.
sources.version_note: Political Analysis 31(3), 2023, pp. 337–351; article DOI and author-posted arXiv full text were checked.

sources.title: Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models
evidence_locations: article §§2–4; methods, main comparisons, prompt and time sensitivity
findings: Personas based on real ANES respondents produced some group means close to the survey, while simulated response variance was too low and many regression relationships differed from the human data.

Small prompt wording changes and model updates over a three-month interval materially changed results, so increasing the number of generated records can narrow Monte Carlo error without fixing bias or distribution mismatch.
limitations: The questions concern political attitudes and feeling thermometers, and the models and access methods are from an earlier generation; effect sizes do not transfer directly to SCE.
It diagnoses synthetic survey replacement more broadly and does not identify the cause of this project's narrow Q9 distribution.
sources.project_use: This is the closest empirical warning for the current mean-versus-dispersion gap. Use it to motivate preregistered distributional and prompt/version sensitivity checks; do not treat its measured variance gap as an expected SCE effect size.
sources.version_note: Political Analysis 32(4), 2024, pp. 401–416; Cambridge article page and open-access PDF checked.

sources.title: Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
evidence_locations: author-hosted PDF §2.2.1, pp. 12–14: mixture calibration and held-out two-stage game
author-hosted PDF pp. 31–32: ground-truth and PPI discussion
findings: The paper illustrates fitting interpretable mixtures of economic-agent types to behavior in known games, then testing the fitted model in a distinct two-stage game.
The calibration-versus-extrapolation separation is useful methodologically: matching behavior in a calibration setting does not itself establish performance in a new setting.
limitations: The paper is an economic-agent framework and game application, not a household inflation-expectation survey or validation of SCE probabilities.

Version dates differ across records: the NBER series lists a February 2026 revision, while the author-hosted PDF inspected here carries a December 7, 2025 cover date. The specific February 2026 version was not verified as the PDF read.
sources.project_use: Borrow the separation of calibration and genuinely held-out tasks. Any learned mixture or prompt choice must be fit only on development months; evaluate against a later sealed SCE month and transparent baselines.
sources.version_note: NBER Working Paper 31122, first issued 2023; NBER metadata reports a February 2026 revision. The opened author-hosted full text is dated 2025-12-07, so this record does not claim to have read the February 2026 revision.

sources.title: Using Large Language Models to Simulate Multiple Humans and Replicate Human Subject Studies
evidence_locations: PDF §§3–5, pp. 1–2: Turing Experiment setup, replication results, Wisdom of Crowds distortion
findings: Across four established human-subject studies, the authors report that simulated participants replicated the main finding in three studies, while one Wisdom of Crowds task showed an over-accuracy distortion.
Replication can reveal task-specific distortions even where a headline aggregate finding appears to match.
limitations: The tested laboratory studies and response formats are not SCE inflation-expectation questions, and the results do not establish fidelity for arbitrary populations or tasks.
The paper does not supply a validated method for mapping generated answer distributions into SCE survey-weighted Q8/Q9 estimands.
sources.project_use: Use task-specific, predeclared checks for plausible distortions and replicate relationships, not a single realism score. The over-accuracy example motivates checking whether generated Q8/Q9 responses are systematically too moderate, too uniform, or too informed.
sources.version_note: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, ICML 2023, pp. 337–371; official PMLR page and PDF checked.

sources.title: LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals
evidence_locations: current arXiv v3 PDF, pp. 1–3: study and sample
PDF pp. 9–10: held-out evaluation and limitations
findings: The study recruited 1,052 U.S. participants for approximately two-hour interviews averaging about 6,491 words, alongside structured surveys; this is much richer input than demographic labels alone.
On held-out GSS items, agents grounded in participants' self-reports reached 82–86% of participants' own two-week test-retest consistency, compared with 74% for demographic-only agents.
The reported individual-level accuracy does not by itself establish that simulated respondents reproduce population-level cross-question correlations or a survey's joint distribution.
limitations: The paper uses extensive person-specific interview data; its main result must not be attributed to 1,000 agents receiving only demographic labels.
The sample is English-speaking and U.S.-based, evaluation uses one model family and specific held-out questions, and the economic-game results do not clearly establish a benefit from self-reports.
It is a preprint with a substantial version/title change: v1 (2024-11) was titled 'Generative Agent Simulations of 1,000 People'; the current v3 was posted 2026-06-28.
sources.project_use: Treat verified, sourced household experience as a candidate input to test against demographic-only profiles. Do not import the individual-level performance claim to this project, whose profiles do not contain comparable interviews, and evaluate population joint structure separately.
sources.version_note: Current version inspected: arXiv v3, posted 2026-06-28, titled 'LLM Agents Grounded in Self-Reports Enable General-Purpose Simulation of Individuals'. The initial v1 title and framing differed; citations to 2024 refer to the first posting year, not the current version date.

sources.title: Do LLMs Play Dice? Exploring Probability Distribution Sampling in Large Language Models for Behavioral Simulation
evidence_locations: current arXiv v3 PDF §§3–5, pp. 3–8: explicit distributions, implicit behavioral distributions, programmatic sampling
findings: The experiments find that models can often identify a requested probability distribution but do not reliably generate samples in accordance with it.
Using Python for explicit distribution sampling improves that task, while complex implicit behavioral distributions remain difficult.
The paper sets temperature to 0.9 to increase sequence diversity; increased text diversity does not establish that samples match a target human distribution.
limitations: The benchmark concerns distribution-sampling tasks and behavioral sequences, not SCE-specific Q9 elicitation or survey weighting.
Tool-based random sampling can implement a declared probability vector but cannot supply evidence that the vector itself is a real respondent's belief.
sources.project_use: Keep the API temperature fixed in economic-input contrasts. If stochastic API variation needs estimation, repeat identical P/E/prompt calls as a separate technical-noise analysis; do not present temperature as a model of household expectation formation.
sources.version_note: Published in Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics (COLING 2025), pp. 5375–5390. The arXiv preprint was first posted 2024-04-13 and v3 posted 2024-12-18; the targeted full-text read was the arXiv v3 PDF, while the official ACL Anthology publication page and PDF URL were checked.

sources.title: How Many Human Survey Respondents is a Large Language Model Worth? An Uncertainty Quantification Perspective
evidence_locations: current author PDF §2.2, pp. 4–7: uncertainty set and calibration
PDF examples: binary survey tasks and empirical coverage
findings: The proposed approach calibrates the effective synthetic sample size using a bank of related questions with human labels and uncertainty coverage checks.
Treating many synthetic responses as independent human observations can create intervals that are too narrow around a biased synthetic mean; too little synthetic weight can leave estimates noisy.
limitations: The method relies on related human-labeled calibration questions and assumptions about transferability/exchangeability and sample independence.

The current examples center on student samples and binary items; this does not directly establish calibration for SCE survey weights, Q8/Q9 paired outcomes, or respondent-level ten-bin probability vectors.
This is a preprint; the current inspected author PDF is dated 2026-06-17, later than the initial 2025 posting.
sources.project_use: Use as a warning that synthetic row count is not effective human sample size. Any interval calibration should be learned from separate labeled tasks or periods and assessed on a sealed target month; 600 calls alone do not identify the effective sample size.
sources.version_note: arXiv:2502.17773; initial post in 2025. The current arXiv v6 was posted 2026-06-15; no journal publication claim is made.

gaps: No selected paper directly validates survey-weighted SCE Q8/Q9 joint distributions or ten-bin within-person subjective densities.
The literature does not identify whether this project's narrow dispersion comes from shared economic information E, demographic-only profiles P, model priors, prompt form, or API sampling noise.
Current model training cutoffs are unknown, so retrospective replay of already public SCE periods cannot be labeled uncontaminated ex-ante prediction.
No local PDF or SHA-256 is present because shell DNS access was blocked by the sandbox; exact source URLs are recorded for parent-task retrieval.
